title: Japan Restaurants Let Diners Pay to Skip the Line
paragraphs: At popular restaurants in Japan, customers sometimes have to wait in line for more than two hours. But now, more and more restaurants are giving people the option to pay extra to skip the line.

One of the main services is called SuiSui. As of September 18, it was being used at 104 restaurants in 20 prefectures across Japan. Most of them are in city centers and tourist areas, where long lines often form.

The system is quite easy to use for most people. Customers scan a QR code outside the restaurant with their smartphone and buy a "fast pass" ticket. The ticket does not reserve a seat, but it lets them go to the front of the line. Prices usually range from 500 to 2,000 yen, depending on the restaurant and how busy it is. At very busy times, the price can be even higher.

For example, at Kyoto Kamosoba Den, a soba noodle restaurant in Kyoto, people often wait more than two hours on weekends and holidays. One couple paid 4,000 yen each to skip the line. Most of the restaurant's fast pass customers are tourists, who want to save time for sightseeing. Hideyuki Shibata, the head of the company that runs the restaurant, said people seem to like the service because they can finish eating early.

The service is also popular with young people in Japan, who care a lot about using their time well. Yusuke Takenouchi, a 29-year-old office worker in Tokyo, has used the service more than ten times at a ramen restaurant near Tokyo Station. He said he cannot get his time back, but he can quickly make up for 500 yen.
Yutaka Suzuki, a researcher at the Distribution Economics Institute of Japan, believes the idea may spread to other places with long waits, such as art museums.
